messages.content:
You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF nominal).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.2 V at nominal: low, so diode drops matter.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 150 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weak excitation; Ip = 30 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 470 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       2.24    2.25    26.2   0.269      15.2  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S2       1.76    1.77    20.3       -      20.7  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S3       5.68    5.72    84.4  0.0779      14.7  ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S4       1.51    1.52    20.8       -      2.27  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S5       2.26    2.28    43.5   0.318      10.9  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S6       1.93    1.94    18.8   0.379      11.3  ok       ok       ok       ok       ok      

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 1.8 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 1 of 12.

This is your first round: choose the structures you think most likely to meet every condition.

Reply with one JSON object only.

reply.reasoning:
*   Goal: Power a sensor-node load $R_L$ from a piezo harvester.
    *   Constraints:
        *   $V_{out\_min} \ge 1.8\text{ V}$
        *   $V_{out\_max} \le 3.6\text{ V}$
        *   $V_{pp} \le 0.05\text{ V}$
        *   $t_{up} \le 0.4\text{ s}$
        *   $\Delta V \le 0.02\text{ V}$ (settled mean output)
    *   Piezo: $I_p \sin(2\pi f t)$, $C_p = 25\text{ nF}$, $R_{leak} = 20\text{ M}\Omega$.
    *   Open-circuit voltage $V_{oc} = I_p / (2\pi f C_p) \approx 3.18\text{ V}$ (nominal).
    *   Operating Conditions (S1-S6): Varying load $R_L$, excitation $I_p$, frequency $f$, and capacitance $C_p$.
    *   Reference Design (FBR) fails:
        *   S2 (heavy load): $V_{avg} = 1.76\text{ V} < 1.8\text{ V}$ (too low).
        *   S3 (strong excitation, light load): $V_{max} = 5.72\text{ V} > 3.6\text{ V}$ (too high), $V_{pp}$ high.
        *   S4 (weak excitation): $V_{avg} = 1.51\text{ V} < 1.8\text{ V}$ (too low).
        *   S5 (low frequency): $\Delta V$ fails (not settled).

    *   The open-circuit voltage is low ($\sim 3\text{ V}$). A full-bridge rectifier (FBR) loses $\sim 0.5\text{ V}$ (two diodes).
    *   $V_{out} = V_{oc} - 2V_{diode}$. If $V_{oc} = 3.2\text{ V}$ and $2V_{diode} = 0.5\text{ V}$, we get $2.7\text{ V}$.
    *   However, for S2 (heavy load) and S4 (weak excitation), FBR fails.
    *   We need a way to increase the voltage or reduce the losses.
    *   Synchronous Switching Harvesting on Inductor (SSHI) or Parallel-SSHI (P-SSHI) can significantly improve the extracted power and voltage from low-$V_{oc}$ piezos by flipping the voltage across $C_p$ at the peaks.

    *   *Strategy 1: Synchronous Switching (SSHI).*
        An inductor $L$ is used to invert the voltage on $C_p$ at the extrema of the oscillation. This increases the effective $V_{oc}$ and power extraction.
        Circuit: Piezo $\rightarrow$ L-S switch $\rightarrow$ Rectifier $\rightarrow$ $C_{out}$.
        Actually, the standard SSHI uses an inductor and a switch to flip the capacitor voltage.

    *   *Strategy 2: Zener Clamp.*
        To prevent $V_{out}$ from exceeding $3.6\text{ V}$ (as in S3), a Zener diode (DZ33) at node `out` is essential.

    *   *Strategy 3: Active Rectification or improved efficiency.*
        Given the low $V_{oc}$, maybe a half-wave rectifier with SSHI or a simplified SSHI structure.

    *   **Topology 1: SSHI-likeVoltage Inversion.**
        Use a switch and an inductor to flip the charge on $C_p$.
        Wait, a simpler version: an inductor $L$ and a switch $S$ in parallel with the piezo, with a rectifier.
        Let's try the "Parallel-SSHI" concept.
        Actually, the most common SSHI:
        - Piezo in parallel with a rectifier.
        - Inductor $L$ and switch $S$ connected to flip $C_p$ voltage.
        Wait, the prompt mentions: "For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp)." This is a huge hint.
        Structure:
        - $C_p$ is flipped by $L$ and $S$ (SYNC).
        - The flipped voltage is then rectified.
        Wait, if we just put the rectifier across the piezo and add the inversion circuit, the inversion circuit helps "push" more charge into the storage capacitor.

    *   **Topology 2: Improved Rectifier + Zener.**
        FBR with a Zener clamp to fix S3's $V_{max}$. But FBR still fails S2 and S4 (too low). We need more voltage.

    *   **Topology 3: Synchronous Charge Extraction (SCE).**
        Use a switch to connect the piezo to the storage capacitor only at the peaks.
        But we have a specific SYNC controller provided.

    *   **Refining SSHI Topology:**
        Piezo nodes: `pzp`, `pzn`.
        Rectifier (FBR):
        D1: `pzp` $\rightarrow$ `out`
        D2: `pzn` $\rightarrow$ `out`
        D3: `0` $\rightarrow$ `pzp`
        D4: `0` $\rightarrow$ `pzn`
        Wait, FBR is 4 diodes.
        SSHI part:
        $L$ and $S$ in parallel with the piezo.
        $L$ from `pzp` to `n1`, $S$ from `n1` to `pzn`.
        $S$ is controlled by SYNC.
        This flips the voltage across the piezo every half-cycle.
        This significantly increases the voltage seen by the rectifier.

    *   **Wait, look at the Reference Design again.**
        FBR fails S2, S4 (too low) and S3 (too high).
        The "too high" is easy: add a Zener clamp `DZ33` from `out` to `0`.
        The "too low" requires increasing efficiency.

    *   **Design A: SSHI (Parallel) + FBR + Zener + $C_{out}$.**
        - Piezo (`pzp`, `pzn`)
        - Rectifier:
            - D1: `pzp` $\rightarrow$ `out` (DSCH)
            - D2: `pzn` $\rightarrow$ `out` (DSCH)
            - D3: `0` $\rightarrow$ `pzp` (DSCH)
            - D4: `0` $\rightarrow$ `pzn` (DSCH)
        - Inversion:
            - L1: `pzp` $\rightarrow$ `n1`
            - S1: `n1` $\rightarrow$ `pzn` (ctrl: G1)
            - G1: `SYNC`, edges: "both", phase: 0.0, ton: $\sim 30\text{ $\mu$s}$ (calculated as $\pi \sqrt{L C_p}$).
        - Protection:
            - D5: `0` $\rightarrow$ `out` (DZ33)
        - Storage:
            - C1: `out` $\rightarrow$ `0`

    *   **Design B: SSHI (Series) / Simple Charge Pump.**
        Maybe a simpler approach?
        Just a half-bridge with the inductor?
        Actually, let's try a different inversion strategy.
        What if we use a switch to connect the piezo to the capacitor at the peaks?
        S1: `pzp` $\rightarrow$ `out` (ctrl: G1, edges: "pos")
        S2: `pzn` $\rightarrow$ `out` (ctrl: G2, edges: "neg")
        This is "Synchronous Charge Extraction". But we need to ensure $V_{out}$ is managed.

    *   **Design C: Half-Bridge Rectifier with SSHI.**
        Half-bridge (two diodes) is often more efficient (lower drop) but captures less energy.
        But combined with SSHI, it might be better.
        Let's stick to Design A as the primary candidate.

    *   $C_p = 25\text{ nF}$.
    *   If $L = 10\text{ mH}$, $T_{inv} = \pi \sqrt{10\text{e-3} \cdot 25\text{e-9}} = \pi \sqrt{250\text{e-12}} = \pi \cdot 15.8\text{ $\mu$s} \approx 50\text{ $\mu$s}$.
    *   If $L = 4.7\text{ mH}$, $T_{inv} = \pi \sqrt{4.7\text{e-3} \cdot 25\text{e-9}} = \pi \cdot 10.8\text{ $\mu$s} \approx 34\text{ $\mu$s}$.
    *   This is within the $t_{on}$ range ($100\text{ ns}$ to $1\text{ ms}$).

    *   D1-D4: Full Bridge (DSCH)
    *   D5: Zener Clamp (DZ33)
    *   C1: Output Cap (e.g., $2.2\text{ $\mu$F}$)
    *   L1: Inversion Inductor
    *   S1: Inversion Switch
    *   G1: SYNC controller (both edges, $t_{on}$ tuned)
    *   Total components: 4 (rect) + 1 (zener) + 1 (cap) + 1 (L) + 1 (S) + 1 (G) = 9 components. (Limit is 16).

    *   L1: `pzp` $\rightarrow$ `n1`
    *   S1: `n1` $\rightarrow$ `pzn` (G1)
    *   D1: `pzp` $\rightarrow$ `out`
    *   D2: `pzn` $\rightarrow$ `out`
    *   D3: `0` $\rightarrow$ `pzp`
    *   D4: `0` $\rightarrow$ `pzn`
    *   D5: `0` $\rightarrow$ `out` (DZ33)
    *   C1: `out` $\rightarrow$ `0`
    *   G1: `SYNC`

    *Self-Correction on FBR:* In a full bridge, the nodes are:
    Bridge input: `pzp`, `pzn`.
    Bridge output: `out`, `0`.
    Diodes:
    1. `pzp` to `out`
    2. `pzn` to `out`
    3. `0` to `pzp`
    4. `0` to `pzn`
    Wait, the standard FBR for a piezo is usually:
    - $D_1$: `pzp` $\rightarrow$ `out`
    - $D_2$: `pzn` $\rightarrow$ `out`
    - $D_3$: `0` $\rightarrow$ `pzp`
    - $D_4$: `0` $\rightarrow$ `pzn`
    Let's check the directions:
    When $V_{pzp} > V_{pzn}$:
    $D_1$ conducts (`pzp` $\rightarrow$ `out`), $D_4$ conducts (`0` $\rightarrow$ `pzn`).
    When $V_{pzn} > V_{pzp}$:
    $D_2$ conducts (`pzn` $\rightarrow$ `out`), $D_3$ conducts (`0` $\rightarrow$ `pzp`).
    This is correct.

    *   $V_{out\_min}$ (S2, S4): The SSHI inversion increases the voltage across the piezo, which helps push more charge through the diodes, increasing $V_{out}$.
    *   $V_{out\_max}$ (S3): The DZ33 zener clamp limits $V_{out}$ to $\sim 3.3\text{ V}$.
    *   $V_{pp}$: $C_{out}$ (e.g., $2.2\text{ $\mu$F}$) should handle ripple.
    *   $t_{up}$: SSHI speeds up charging.

    Wait, I should propose a second topology just in case. Maybe a half-bridge with the same SSHI? Or a different SYNC config?
    Let's try:
    1. SSHI + FBR + Zener (The most robust).
    2. SSHI + Half-Bridge + Zener (Lower diode drop).
    3. A simpler "Charge Extraction" using switches instead of diodes.

    Wait, the "Charge Extraction" (SCE) using switches:
    - S1: `pzp` $\rightarrow$ `out` (G1, edges: "pos")
    - S2: `pzn` $\rightarrow$ `out` (G2, edges: "neg")
    - C1: `out` $\rightarrow$ `0`
    - D1: `0` $\rightarrow$ `out` (DZ33)
    - L1/S3: SSHI inversion (as above).
    This eliminates diode drops entirely.

    *Let's check SCE feasibility:*
    S1 closes at the positive peak of $V_{pzp}$. $C_p$ is connected to $C_{out}$. Charge flows from $C_p$ to $C_{out}$ if $V_{pzp} > V_{out}$.
    This is very efficient but only if $V_{pzp}$ can actually exceed $V_{out}$. With SSHI, $V_{pzp}$ is boosted, so this is possible.

    However, let's stick to the most common and reliable ones first.

    Topology 1: SSHI + FBR + Zener.
    Topology 2: SSHI + Half-Bridge + Zener.
    Topology 3: SCE + SSHI + Zener.

    Wait, I'll refine Topology 2 to be slightly different. A half-bridge only uses 2 diodes.
    Half-bridge:
    D1: `pzp` $\rightarrow$ `out`
    D2: `0` $\rightarrow$ `pzn` (Wait, no. $D_1$ `pzp` $\rightarrow$ `out`, $D_2$ `pzn` $\rightarrow$ `out` is not a half-bridge).
    A half-bridge is:
    $D_1$: `pzp` $\rightarrow$ `out`
    $C_{out}$: `out` $\rightarrow$ `0`
    (Charge only flows when `pzp` is positive).
    Combined with SSHI inversion, you can still get power on both half-cycles because the inversion flips the charge.

    Let's go with:
    1. `sshi_fbr_zener`
    2. `sshi_half_zener`
    3. `sshi_sce_zener` (using switches for rectification)

    *Actually*, let's keep it simpler. I'll provide the SSHI + FBR + Zener and a variation.

    *Self-Correction on SSHI:*
    The inversion happens at the *peaks* of the voltage. The `SYNC` controller "closes its switches... at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero crossings of the piezo current."
    This is exactly what's needed for SSHI.

    - L1: $4.7\text{ mH}$
    - C1: $2.2\text{ $\mu$F}$
    - G1: $t_{on} = 3.4\text{e-05}$, edges = "both", phase = 0.0.
    - Diodes: DSCH for bridge, DZ33 for clamp.
